4096 elements (cached):  plain loop 4.38 µs,  @simd 0.28 µs
4M elements, plain loop, SoA  25.42 ms
4M elements, @simd, SoA       2.3 ms
4M elements, sum, SoA         5.36 ms
4M elements, @simd, AoS       21.02 ms

choices: Splitting the sum into lanes changes its rounding, which needs permission
Vector registers cannot hold `Float64` values
The bounds checks on `x[i]` stay in the loop and block the vector instructions
questions.explain: Four lanes compute four partial sums and add them at the end: a different order of additions, so different last digits (floating-point addition is not associative). The compiler preserves your results unless `@simd` (or `@fastmath`) allows reassociation. `eachindex` already lets it drop the bounds checks.
misconceptions: AVX2 registers hold four `Float64` and AVX-512 eight; the `a[i] = b[i] + c[i]` loop is vectorized with them without any annotation.
`eachindex(x)` produces only valid indices, so the compiler removes the checks by itself; what remains is the dependency of each `s` on the previous one.
questions.prompt: Without `@simd`, why does the compiler not vectorize `for i in eachindex(x); s += x[i]; end` for a `Vector{Float64}`?

choices: Nothing for speed, since both layouts hold the same numbers in the same cache
It makes the loop safe to run on several threads
It reads one eighth of the memory, in contiguous vector loads
It removes the need for `@simd` on the reduction
questions.explain: In the AoS, consecutive `x` values are 64 bytes apart, so every cache line loaded carries one useful number. In the SoA each line carries eight `x` values, and the vector unit loads them in one instruction. The reduction still needs `@simd` to be reordered.
misconceptions: The numbers are the same, but the memory traffic is not: the loop moves whole cache lines, and in the AoS seven eighths of each line is fields it does not use.
Reading is race-free in either layout; layout changes speed, not thread safety.
Contiguous data makes vector loads possible, but reordering the sum still changes its rounding, so the compiler still needs `@simd`'s permission.
questions.prompt: A simulation stores particles as a `Vector{Particle}` with 8 `Float64` fields, and its hot loop reads only the `x` field of every particle. What does switching to one vector per field (struct of arrays) change for that loop?

sections.title: SIMD and data layout

sections.body:
A core can do arithmetic much faster than memory can deliver operands. So
each loop has two possible limits, and the lower one wins. The **roofline
model** ([Williams, Waterman and Patterson 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roofline_model))
states it as

    attainable FLOP/s = min(peak FLOP/s,  I × bandwidth)

where the **arithmetic intensity** `I` is the number of floating-point
operations per byte moved between memory and the core. Two kernels on
arrays too large for the caches:

* **The stream triad** `a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i]` does 2 flops and asks for
  24 bytes (read `b[i]` and `c[i]`, write `a[i]`): `I = 1/12` flop per byte.
  At a bandwidth of 10 GB/s it cannot exceed about 0.8 GFLOP/s, a small
  fraction of what one core can compute. It is **bandwidth-bound**. (Most
  caches read a line before writing into it, "write-allocate", so the
  hardware moves 32 bytes per element; a GB/s figure computed from 24 bytes
  is a quarter lower than the real traffic.)
* **A degree-64 polynomial** evaluated by Horner's rule at each `b[i]` does
  128 flops (64 multiply-adds) and moves 16 bytes: `I = 8`. Memory is not
  its limit; the core is. Here it is not even the core's peak: each
  multiply-add needs the previous one's result, the same chain as
  `s += x[i]` in the first section, so the loop runs at one multiply-add per
  latency of that instruction, a small fraction of the peak. It is
  **latency-bound**, which for threads behaves like compute-bound: each core
  runs its own chains.

What this predicts for threads: a second core doubles the arithmetic but
not the memory bandwidth, which the cores share. A kernel limited inside the
core can nearly double its speed on two threads; a bandwidth-bound one gains
only as much as one core was failing to use of the memory system. One core
often draws a large share of the bandwidth on its own, so the triad's
speedup is below 2 by an amount that depends on the machine, which is why
the example measures it instead of asserting it.

examples.caption: Arithmetic intensity of the two kernels from their flop and byte counts, and the bandwidth-bound ceiling each would have at an assumed 10 GB/s (the assumption is only for the arithmetic).
examples.code:
kernels = (("triad    a[i] = b[i] + s*c[i]", 2, 3 * 8), ("Horner-64 a[i] = p(b[i])  ", 128, 2 * 8))
for (name, flops, bytes) in kernels
    I = flops / bytes
    println(name, "  I = ", rpad(round(I; digits = 3), 6), " flop/byte,  ceiling at 10 GB/s: ",
            round(I * 10; digits = 2), " GFLOP/s")
end
examples.notice: Notice the factor of 96 between the intensities: the triad's ceiling at 10 GB/s is below 1 GFLOP/s, while the polynomial's is 80 GFLOP/s, more than a chain of dependent multiply-adds can reach, so its limit is in the core.
examples.output:
triad    a[i] = b[i] + s*c[i]  I = 0.083  flop/byte,  ceiling at 10 GB/s: 0.83 GFLOP/s
Horner-64 a[i] = p(b[i])    I = 8.0    flop/byte,  ceiling at 10 GB/s: 80.0 GFLOP/s

examples.caption: The triad on 8 million elements and the polynomial on 1 million, timed with 1 and 2 tasks in a Julia started with 2 threads. Recorded, not checked: the numbers depend on the CPU, its memory and what else the machine is running.
examples.code:
write("roofline.jl", raw"""
using Base.Threads
function triad!(a, b, c, s, r)
    @inbounds @simd for i in r
        a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i]
    end
end
function horner!(a, b, r)
    @inbounds for i in r
        x = b[i]
        y = 0.0
        for k in 1:64
            y = muladd(y, x, 1.0)
        end
        a[i] = y
    end
end
function on_tasks(f, ntasks, n)            # ntasks contiguous chunks, one task each
    @sync for r in Iterators.partition(1:n, cld(n, ntasks))
        @spawn f(r)
    end
end
best(f) = (f(); minimum(@elapsed(f()) for _ in 1:5))
n, m = 2^23, 2^20                         # triad on 8M elements (far beyond the caches), Horner on 1M
a, b, c = zeros(n), rand(n), rand(n)
println("threads: ", nthreads())
for (name, k, flops, bytes, len) in (("triad ", r -> triad!(a, b, c, 3.0, r), 2, 24, n),
                                     ("Horner", r -> horner!(a, b, r), 128, 16, m))
    t1 = best(() -> on_tasks(k, 1, len))
    t2 = best(() -> on_tasks(k, 2, len))
    println(name, "  1 thread: ", round(bytes * len / t1 / 1e9; digits = 1), " GB/s, ",
            round(flops * len / t1 / 1e9; digits = 1), " GFLOP/s;  speedup on 2 threads: ", round(t1 / t2; digits = 2))
end
""")
run(`$(Base.julia_cmd()) --threads=2 roofline.jl`);
examples.notice: Notice the triad's GB/s (counted at 24 bytes per element, so a quarter below the real traffic): it is the memory system's speed, and the model predicts a speedup below 2 for it, by a machine-dependent amount. For the polynomial it predicts close to 2 on two real cores, since each computes its half independently. Two hyperthreads of one core share its arithmetic, and a busy machine takes time and bandwidth from both kernels, so a measurement can fall short of either prediction; rerun to compare.
examples.output:
threads: 2
triad   1 thread: 17.4 GB/s, 1.5 GFLOP/s;  speedup on 2 threads: 1.44
Horner  1 thread: 0.6 GB/s, 4.7 GFLOP/s;  speedup on 2 threads: 2.02

choices: A speedup near 2, since the iterations are independent and split evenly in two
A speedup bounded by how much more memory bandwidth two cores get
No change at all, since threads cannot share one array
questions.explain: Axpy does 2 flops per 24 bytes (read `x[i]` and `y[i]`, write `y[i]`), `I = 1/12`: bandwidth-bound. Two cores share the memory bus, so the speedup is the ratio of the bandwidth two cores draw to what one draws, often well under 2 and machine-dependent.
misconceptions: Independent iterations make the loop safe to split, but both halves still wait on the same memory system; the arithmetic was never the limit.
Threads share memory, and splitting the index range between them is race-free; the gain is small because memory is the limit, not because sharing fails.
questions.prompt: A kernel computes `y[i] = a * x[i] + y[i]` (axpy) on vectors of 100 million `Float64`. On two threads instead of one, what does the roofline model predict?

sections.title: Memory bandwidth and the roofline

sections.body:
Julia offers three levels for splitting a loop over threads:

* **`Threads.@threads for ...`** splits the iteration range into one chunk
  per thread. Good for a loop whose iterations write to separate places.
* **`Threads.@spawn`** starts one task per piece of work, which the
  scheduler places on any thread; you choose the chunks and combine the
  results yourself (unit 18).
* **OhMyThreads.jl** packages the per-chunk pattern: `tmap(f, xs)` and
  `tmapreduce(f, op, xs)` split `xs` into contiguous chunks, one task each
  (by default as many as threads), reduce each chunk, then combine the
  partial results in order. Its documentation requires `op` to be
  associative and says that "each chunk consists of contiguous elements and
  order is maintained" ([OhMyThreads API](https://juliafolds2.github.io/OhMyThreads.jl/stable/refs/api/)).

One pattern looks race-free and still runs slowly: per-thread accumulators
in neighbouring slots of one array, `acc[t] += x[i]`. No two tasks write
the same element, so the result is right. But caches move memory in lines
of typically 64 bytes, and when one core writes its slot, the line holding
the other core's slot is invalidated too, so the two cores pass the line
back and forth on every write. That is **false sharing**
([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_sharing)). Padding the
slots apart removes it: 128 bytes rather than 64, because many CPUs also
fetch the neighbouring line of each line they load, so two adjacent lines
can still interfere. A local variable per task, returned at the end,
removes the shared array altogether.

A pattern from older code is unsafe: indexing buffers by
`Threads.threadid()`. The Julia manual says `threadid()` "should not be
treated as constant within a task" and "Buffers should not be managed
based on `threadid()`" ([multi-threading manual](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1.10/manual/multi-threading/)):
a task can move to another thread, and two tasks on one thread can share the
buffer.

examples.caption: `tmapreduce` with 1, 2 and 4 tasks against a serial `mapreduce` (on this site's single thread the tasks take turns, but the chunking is the same as on many threads).
examples.code:
using OhMyThreads, Random
x = randn(Xoshiro(3), 10^6)
serial = mapreduce(abs2, +, x)
for nt in (1, 2, 4)
    r = tmapreduce(abs2, +, x; ntasks = nt)
    println("ntasks = ", nt, ": ", round(r; sigdigits = 12), "   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): ", isapprox(r, serial; rtol = 1e-14))
end
examples.notice: Notice that the threaded results agree with the serial one to a relative `1e-14`. They are printed to 12 digits because the last digits are not fixed: each number of tasks adds the terms in another order, each chunk is summed with SIMD instructions whose width depends on the CPU, and the next section shows chunkings whose last digits differ.
examples.output:
ntasks = 1: 999655.955579   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): true
ntasks = 2: 999655.955579   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): true
ntasks = 4: 999655.955579   ≈ serial (rtol 1e-14): true

examples.caption: False sharing on 2 threads: each task adds its half of a small vector, 1000 times over, into its own slot of a shared array, with the two slots adjacent (one cache line) or 128 bytes apart, against a local variable per task. Recorded, not checked: timings vary between runs and CPUs.
examples.code:
write("false_sharing.jl", raw"""
using Base.Threads
function slot_sum(x, stride, reps)          # task t accumulates into acc[(t - 1) * stride + 1]
    acc = zeros(2 * stride)
    h = length(x) ÷ 2
    @sync for t in 1:2
        @spawn begin
            j = (t - 1) * stride + 1
            for _ in 1:reps, i in (t - 1) * h + 1:t * h
                @inbounds acc[j] += x[i]
            end
        end
    end
    return acc[1] + acc[stride + 1]
end
function local_sum(x, reps)
    h = length(x) ÷ 2
    tasks = [@spawn begin
                 s = 0.0
                 for _ in 1:reps, i in (t - 1) * h + 1:t * h
                     @inbounds s += x[i]
                 end
                 s
             end for t in 1:2]
    return fetch(tasks[1]) + fetch(tasks[2])
end
x = rand(2^14)                              # 128 KB: stays in cache, so memory speed does not hide the effect
best(f) = (f(); minimum(@elapsed(f()) for _ in 1:5))
println("threads: ", nthreads(), "; same sums: ", slot_sum(x, 1, 2) == slot_sum(x, 16, 2) == local_sum(x, 2))
println("adjacent slots (one cache line): ", round(best(() -> slot_sum(x, 1, 1000)) * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
println("slots 128 bytes apart:           ", round(best(() -> slot_sum(x, 16, 1000)) * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
println("a local variable per task:       ", round(best(() -> local_sum(x, 1000)) * 1e3; digits = 1), " ms")
""")
run(`$(Base.julia_cmd()) --threads=2 false_sharing.jl`);
examples.notice: Notice that all three give the same sum. On two separate cores the adjacent slots should be the slowest, since every write by one core takes the cache line away from the other; padding should help, and the local variable should be fastest because it never touches shared memory inside the loop. If the two threads land on hyperthreads of one core, they share its cache and the effect can vanish; a machine busy with other work can swamp it too. Rerun to compare.
examples.output:
threads: 2; same sums: true
adjacent slots (one cache line): 8.9 ms
slots 128 bytes apart:           8.8 ms
a local variable per task:       8.9 ms

choices: The two tasks write the same element, so updates are lost
`Vector{Float64}` is not thread-safe, so Julia takes a lock around each element write
Both slots sit on one cache line, which the cores keep taking from each other
questions.explain: Each task writes only its own element, so there is no race. But the two elements are 8 bytes apart, inside one 64-byte cache line, and a write by one core invalidates that line in the other core's cache. Padding the slots apart or keeping the sum in a local variable fixes it.
misconceptions: Lost updates would make the result wrong; here each task owns one element. The cost is in the hardware's cache coherence, not in the program's logic.
Julia adds no locks to array writes; arrays are not thread-safe, which is why races are the programmer's job. The slowdown comes from the cache line both slots live on.
questions.prompt: Two tasks each sum half of a vector into `acc[1]` and `acc[2]` of a shared `Vector{Float64}`. The result is correct but slower than on one thread. Why?

sections.title: Threads in practice: OhMyThreads and false sharing

sections.body:
A parallel reduction with `p` chunks computes `p` partial sums and then adds
them. That is a different parenthesization of the same sum, so by unit 30's
rule it rounds differently. Three consequences:

* **The result depends on the number of chunks.** With OhMyThreads' default
  of one chunk per thread, the same program gives different last digits on 2
  and on 8 threads. For a fixed number of chunks the result is repeatable,
  because the partial sums are combined in chunk order.
* **None of the answers is "the" right one.** Each is a different rounding
  of the true sum, and all obey the same bound: the error of summing `n`
  terms in any order is at most about `(n - 1) u` times `sum(abs, x)`, with
  `u = eps() / 2`. With `p` chunks the worst-case bound shrinks to about
  `(n/p + p - 2) u sum(abs, x)`, since each term passes through a shorter
  chain of additions. That is a bound, not a prediction: random rounding
  errors mostly cancel, and in the example below the measured errors do not
  shrink steadily as the chunks get more numerous.
* **Tests must compare with a tolerance**, derived from that bound, never
  with `==` against a serial run. The tolerance is relative to
  `sum(abs, x)`, not to the sum: with cancellation the sum can be much
  smaller than the terms.

The example below uses a plain loop for each chunk, so its digits depend
only on the chunking and are the same on every machine.

examples.caption: One million `randn` terms summed with 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 contiguous chunks (a plain loop per chunk, partial sums added in order), against the exact sum computed in `BigFloat`.
examples.code:
using Random
x = randn(Xoshiro(7), 10^6)
function chunked_sum(x, nchunks)
    total = 0.0
    for r in Iterators.partition(eachindex(x), cld(length(x), nchunks))
        s = 0.0
        for i in r
            s += x[i]
        end
        total += s
    end
    return total
end
exact = sum(big.(x))
bound = (length(x) - 1) * eps() / 2 * sum(abs, x)
println("bound on the error: ", round(bound; sigdigits = 2))
for nc in (1, 2, 3, 4, 8)
    s = chunked_sum(x, nc)
    println(rpad(nc, 2), "chunks: ", rpad(s, 22), " error ", rpad(round(Float64(abs(s - exact)); sigdigits = 2), 9),
            " within bound: ", abs(s - exact) <= bound)
end
examples.notice: Notice that the five chunkings give different floats, every one of them within the bound `(n - 1) u sum(abs, x)`, and that the error is far below the bound (rounding errors of random sign mostly cancel).
examples.output:
bound on the error: 8.9e-5
1 chunks: 293.1599232981022      error 2.3e-11   within bound: true
2 chunks: 293.1599232981044      error 2.5e-11   within bound: true
3 chunks: 293.159923298084       error 4.9e-12   within bound: true
4 chunks: 293.1599232981043      error 2.5e-11   within bound: true
8 chunks: 293.1599232980958      error 1.7e-11   within bound: true

questions.explain: In one chunk, `1.0 + 1e-16` rounds to `1.0` (below half the spacing `eps() = 2.2e-16`), twice, and `-1.0` cancels it to `0.0`. In two chunks the second chunk is `1e-16 - 1.0`, which rounds to `-prevfloat(1.0) = -(1 - 1.1e-16)`; adding it to `1.0` gives `1.1e-16`. The true sum is `2e-16`, and neither order gets it.
misconceptions: The second chunk does not round the same way: `1e-16 - 1.0` lands next to `-1.0`, where floats are spaced `1.1e-16` apart, so it rounds to `-(1 - 1.1e-16)`, not to `-1.0`.
That is the exact sum; both orders lose digits to rounding against the large terms, and they lose different digits.
The orders are swapped: the single chain rounds both small terms away against `1.0` before the cancellation.
questions.prompt: Four numbers summed in one chunk and in two. What does this print?

choices: `==`, since both add the same numbers
`isapprox` with `rtol = eps()`
`abs(a - b) <= 2(n - 1) * (eps() / 2) * sum(abs, x)`
Compare only the first 8 printed digits, since the rest is rounding noise
questions.explain: Each order's error is at most `(n - 1) u sum(abs, x)`, so two orders differ by at most twice that. The bound is relative to `sum(abs, x)`, which matters when terms cancel: then the sum is small and a relative tolerance on it is far too tight.
misconceptions: The same numbers in a different order round differently; `==` fails as soon as the chunking changes, for example on a machine with more threads.
One `eps` is the error of a single operation; a million additions can each contribute one, and with cancellation the sum is small compared with the terms.
A fixed number of digits ignores cancellation: if the terms nearly cancel, the first 8 digits of the sum may already be rounding noise, and the check fails on a correct program.
questions.prompt: A test checks a threaded `tmapreduce(+, ...)` sum of a million terms against a serial loop. Which check is right?

sections.title: Why a threaded sum changes its last digits

sections.body:
**Amdahl's law** ([Amdahl 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amdahl%27s_law))
asks: for a **fixed problem**, how much faster is it on `p` processors? If a
fraction `f` of the one-processor run time parallelizes perfectly and the
rest `1 - f` does not,

    S_A(p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p),     S_A(∞) = 1 / (1 - f)

A program that is 90% parallel never runs more than 10 times faster, on any
number of cores. The serial part includes everything that does not split:
setup, I/O, a reduction's final combine, the time to start tasks.

**Gustafson's law** ([Gustafson 1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustafson%27s_law))
asks another question: with `p` processors, **how much more work** can you
do in the same time? Here `s` is the serial fraction of the run time
measured **on the `p`-processor run**, and the scaled speedup is

    S_G(p) = s + (1 - s) p

It grows without limit, because the parallel part is assumed to grow with
`p` (a finer grid, more samples) while the serial part stays the same.

The two laws do not contradict each other: they describe different
experiments, and their `s` are measured differently. A job with serial
fraction `s` on `p` processors had serial fraction
`s / (s + (1 - s) p)` when run on one; put that into Amdahl's formula and it
gives Gustafson's number. Use Amdahl when the problem size is fixed (a
given simulation, faster) and Gustafson when the time budget is fixed (a
bigger simulation, in the same time).

The models also say how to read a measurement. A measured speedup `S` on
`p` threads implies an effective serial fraction
`e = (1/S - 1/p) / (1 - 1/p)`, Amdahl's formula solved for the serial
fraction, known as the **Karp-Flatt metric**
([Karp and Flatt 1990](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karp%E2%80%93Flatt_metric)). If `e` grows with
`p`, the loss is not a fixed serial part but an overhead that grows with
the threads, such as shared memory bandwidth.

examples.caption: Amdahl's speedup for three parallel fractions, and Gustafson's for the same numbers read as serial shares of the parallel run.
examples.code:
amdahl(f, p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p)
gustafson(s, p) = s + (1 - s) * p
println("parallel fraction f   p = 2    p = 8    p = 64   p = ∞")
for f in (0.5, 0.9, 0.99)
    println(rpad(f, 22), join((rpad(round(amdahl(f, p); digits = 2), 9) for p in (2, 8, 64)), ""),
            round(1 / (1 - f); digits = 1))
end
println("serial share s (Gustafson)")
for s in (0.5, 0.1, 0.01)
    println(rpad(s, 22), join((rpad(round(gustafson(s, p); digits = 2), 9) for p in (2, 8, 64)), ""), "∞")
end
println("Amdahl with s converted to one processor equals Gustafson: ",
        all(amdahl(1 - s / (s + (1 - s) * p), p) ≈ gustafson(s, p) for s in (0.5, 0.1, 0.01), p in (2, 8, 64)))
examples.notice: Notice the ceilings in the last column: a 99%-parallel program is capped at 100x. Gustafson's numbers grow linearly with `p` instead, because they answer a different question (more work in the same time).
examples.output:
parallel fraction f   p = 2    p = 8    p = 64   p = ∞
0.5                   1.33     1.78     1.97     2.0
0.9                   1.82     4.71     8.77     10.0
0.99                  1.98     7.48     39.26    100.0
serial share s (Gustafson)
0.5                   1.5      4.5      32.5     ∞
0.1                   1.9      7.3      57.7     ∞
0.01                  1.99     7.93     63.37    ∞
Amdahl with s converted to one processor equals Gustafson: true

examples.caption: A program with a serial part (a recurrence, each step of which needs the previous one) and a parallel part (the Horner kernel): Amdahl's prediction for 2 threads from the measured one-thread fraction, against the measured speedup. Recorded, not checked: timings vary.
examples.code:
write("amdahl.jl", raw"""
using Base.Threads, Random
function horner!(a, b, r)
    @inbounds for i in r
        x = b[i]
        y = 0.0
        for k in 1:64
            y = muladd(y, x, 1.0)
        end
        a[i] = y
    end
end
function logistic(x, m)                                   # each step needs the previous one: serial
    for _ in 1:m
        x = 3.7 * x * (1 - x)
    end
    return x
end
function job(b, a, ntasks)
    x = logistic(0.3, 5_000_000)                          # the serial stage
    @sync for r in Iterators.partition(eachindex(b), cld(length(b), ntasks))
        @spawn horner!(a, b, r)                           # the parallel stage
    end
    return x
end
n = 2^20
a, b = zeros(n), rand(Xoshiro(1), n)
const sink = Ref(0.0)                                     # results are used, so no call is optimized away
best(f) = (f(); minimum(@elapsed(sink[] += f()) for _ in 1:5))
t_serial = best(() -> logistic(0.3, 5_000_000))
t1 = best(() -> job(b, a, 1))
t2 = best(() -> job(b, a, 2))
f = 1 - t_serial / t1
S = t1 / t2
amdahl(f, p) = 1 / ((1 - f) + f / p)
println("threads: ", nthreads(), "; measured parallel fraction f = ", round(f; digits = 3))
println("Amdahl predicts S(2) = ", round(amdahl(f, 2); digits = 2), "; measured S(2) = ", round(S; digits = 2))
println("serial fraction implied by S(2): ", round((1 / S - 1 / 2) / (1 - 1 / 2); digits = 3),
        "; measured directly: ", round(1 - f; digits = 3))
println("model only, not measured: S(8) = ", round(amdahl(f, 8); digits = 1), ", S(∞) = ", round(1 / (1 - f); digits = 1))
""")
run(`$(Base.julia_cmd()) --threads=2 amdahl.jl`);
examples.notice: Notice how the prediction from `f` compares with the measured speedup, and the serial fraction implied by the measurement (the Karp-Flatt metric) with the one measured directly. Where they differ, the gap is the overhead Amdahl's model leaves out: starting tasks, shared caches, hyperthreads, or other programs taking the CPU. Anything beyond 2 threads in the last line is the model, not a measurement.
examples.output:
threads: 2; measured parallel fraction f = 0.699
Amdahl predicts S(2) = 1.54; measured S(2) = 1.44
serial fraction implied by S(2): 0.391; measured directly: 0.301
model only, not measured: S(8) = 2.6, S(∞) = 3.3

choices: At most 20 on any number of cores, and about 15 on 64
About 64, since 95% of the work is parallel
About 61, from Gustafson's scaled speedup `s + (1 - s) p` with `s = 0.05`
questions.explain: `S = 1 / (0.05 + 0.95/64) ≈ 15.4`, and no number of cores passes `1/0.05 = 20`: the serial 5% alone takes 1/20 of the original time. Gustafson's 61 answers how much **bigger** a problem 64 cores can do in the same time, which is not this question.
misconceptions: The serial 5% runs at one core's speed however many cores there are; it alone takes 1/20 of the original time.
Gustafson's formula assumes the parallel work grows with the cores; for a fixed problem the serial part is a growing share of the run, and Amdahl's law applies.
questions.prompt: A fixed-size simulation spends 5% of its one-core run time in serial setup. Its author buys a 64-core machine. What does Amdahl's law say about the speedup?

sections.title: Amdahl and Gustafson: two models of speedup

sections.body:
Unit 18's section "Beyond one process: Distributed and GPUs" introduced
worker **processes**: `addprocs`, `@everywhere` and `pmap` from the
Distributed standard library. One more call is used here:
`remotecall_fetch(f, id, args...)` runs `f` on worker `id` and returns the
result ([Distributed manual](https://docs.julialang.org/en/v1.10/stdlib/Distributed/)).
Each worker has its own memory, so arguments are **copied** to it and
results copied back: a worker that mutates an argument mutates its copy.
That costs time per call, so processes pay off for large independent jobs
(a parameter sweep, an ensemble of long simulations), and they are the only
way to use more than one machine. Starting a worker is a new Julia process,
which takes seconds; the example starts one on this machine.

**GPUs** run one small function, a **kernel**, for every index of a range,
in groups of threads (workgroups) that share fast memory. The kernel sees
only its own index and must not depend on the order in which indices run.
KernelAbstractions.jl writes such kernels once and runs them on several
backends: `@kernel` defines it, `@index(Global)` gives the work item's
index, and `kernel(backend, workgroupsize)(args...; ndrange = n)` launches
it ([KernelAbstractions quickstart](https://juliagpu.github.io/KernelAbstractions.jl/v0.9/quickstart/)).
The `CPU()` backend runs the same kernel on the CPU's threads, so a kernel
can be written and tested without a GPU; CUDA.jl, AMDGPU.jl and Metal.jl
provide the GPU backends (not installed here). The roofline applies to GPUs
too: they have far more arithmetic and more bandwidth than a CPU, and a
bandwidth-bound kernel is still bandwidth-bound there.

examples.caption: One worker process: its id, a `pmap` over it, and what happens when a worker mutates an argument.
examples.code:
using Distributed
ENV["JULIA_WORKER_TIMEOUT"] = "200"            # seconds a new worker waits to connect (default 60), for busy machines
println("new workers: ", addprocs(1))
@everywhere square_where(x) = (x^2, myid())
println(pmap(square_where, 1:4))
v = [1, 2, 3]
w = remotecall_fetch(u -> (u[1] = 100; u), 2, v)
println("worker's copy: ", w, "   this process: ", v)
rmprocs(workers());
examples.notice: Notice that every element of the `pmap` ran on worker 2, and that the vector `v` in this process is unchanged after the worker set its first element to 100: the worker received a copy.

examples.caption: The stream triad as a KernelAbstractions kernel on the `CPU()` backend, checked against the broadcast `b .+ s .* c`.
examples.code:
using KernelAbstractions, Random
@kernel function triad_kernel!(a, @Const(b), @Const(c), s)
    i = @index(Global)
    @inbounds a[i] = b[i] + s * c[i]
end
n = 10^6
b, c = rand(Xoshiro(1), n), rand(Xoshiro(2), n)
a = similar(b)
backend = get_backend(a)                      # CPU() for an ordinary Array
triad_kernel!(backend, 256)(a, b, c, 3.0; ndrange = n)
KernelAbstractions.synchronize(backend)
println("backend: ", typeof(backend), "; equals the broadcast: ", a == b .+ 3.0 .* c)
examples.notice: Notice that the kernel's result equals the broadcast exactly: each work item computes `b[i] + s * c[i]` with the same two roundings, and no reduction is involved, so the order of indices cannot change any digit.
examples.output: backend: CPU; equals the broadcast: true

choices: It is doubled, since the worker shares the caller's memory
Julia raises an error, since arguments sent to workers are read-only
Nothing; the worker doubled its own copy of `A`, which stays there
questions.explain: Workers are separate processes: `A` is serialized, sent, and rebuilt in the worker's memory. The worker's `A .*= 2` changes that copy; return the result to get it back. Sending a large matrix each call also costs time, which is why processes suit large, independent jobs.
misconceptions: Threads share memory; processes do not. Distributed copies the argument to the worker.
Nothing makes the copy read-only; the worker mutates it freely, and the change stays on the worker.
questions.prompt: A function called on a worker with `remotecall_fetch(f, 2, A)` does `A .*= 2` on a large matrix `A`. What happens to `A` in the calling process?

choices: Work items run concurrently in no fixed order, so the updates race
Kernels may read their array arguments but never write to any of them
`@index(Global)` gives each work item the same index
questions.explain: A kernel is a function of one index, run for all indices concurrently in groups. Every work item doing a read-modify-write on `total[1]` is the data race of unit 18, on thousands of threads. Reductions on GPUs are written as per-group partial sums combined in a second step, or with atomics.
misconceptions: The triad kernel writes `a[i]`; writes are fine as long as each work item writes its own element.
Each work item gets its own index, which is what makes `a[i] = ...` race-free; the problem is many items writing one element.
questions.prompt: Why may a KernelAbstractions kernel not accumulate into one shared scalar with `total[1] += x[i]`?

sections.title: Beyond threads: worker processes and GPU-style kernels

units.summary: What decides how fast numerical code can run on one core and on several: SIMD and data layout, memory bandwidth and the roofline model, false sharing, threads with OhMyThreads, why a threaded sum changes its last digits, Amdahl's and Gustafson's laws checked against two-thread measurements, worker processes with Distributed, and KernelAbstractions as the CPU model of a GPU kernel.
units.title: Parallel computing and its limits

hints: The starter gives only the first dose. The others are jumps in the gut amount at known times, which is what a `DiscreteCallback` is for.
The callback's condition is checked only where a step ends; tell `solve` with `tstops` to end steps at the dose times, and add `dose` to `integrator.u[1]` there.
problems.prompt:
A one-compartment model with first-order absorption has a gut amount
`A_g` and a central amount `A_c`:

    A_g' = -k_a A_g,     A_c' = k_a A_g - (CL / V) A_c,     C = A_c / V

Write `dosed_concentration(dose, tau, ndoses, ka, CL, V, tq)` that gives
`ndoses` doses of `dose` mg into the gut at `t = 0, tau, 2tau, …`, solves
the model with OrdinaryDiffEq (`abstol = 1e-12`, `reltol = 1e-10`), and
returns the concentration `C(tq)` as a `Float64`. Doses after `tq` do not
matter; `tq` is never exactly a dose time, and the amount at `tq` stays far
above the solver's absolute tolerance (the random cases put `tq` at most
`5 V / CL` hours after the last dose before it).

```julia
dosed_concentration(100.0, 12.0, 1, 1.5, 5.0, 20.0, 6.0)   # one dose
dosed_concentration(100.0, 12.0, 5, 1.5, 5.0, 20.0, 50.0)  # five doses every 12 h
```

Results are compared with `rtol = 1e-6`: at these tolerances, and with a
concentration far above `abstol`, the solver's global error is about
`1e-9` relative (unit 31: one to two digits above `reltol`), so any
correct method, including the exact superposition of single-dose
solutions, agrees far inside that. (Long after the last dose, when the
amount falls below `abstol = 1e-12`, the solver returns noise of that
size, and a relative comparison would mean nothing.)
problems.starter:
using OrdinaryDiffEq

function dosed_concentration(dose, tau, ndoses, ka, CL, V, tq)
    f!(du, u, p, t) = (du[1] = -ka * u[1]; du[2] = ka * u[1] - CL / V * u[2])
    prob = ODEProblem(f!, [dose, 0.0], (0.0, tq))
    sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-12, reltol = 1e-10)
    return sol.u[end][2] / V
end
problems.title: Repeated doses with a callback

hints: The starter uses the linear trapezoid everywhere. On a falling stretch, integrate the exponential that passes through the two samples instead.
Decide per interval: a fall to a positive value gets `(c1 - c2) Δt / log(c1 / c2)`; anything else keeps the linear rule. Check the lengths before the loop.
problems.prompt:
Write `auc_linlog(t, c)` for sample times `t` (increasing) and
concentrations `c` (non-negative), both `Vector{Float64}` of the same
length, that returns the area under the sampled curve as a `Float64`, one
interval at a time:

* if the concentration **falls** to a **nonzero** value (`c2 < c1` and
  `c2 > 0`): the log trapezoid `(c1 - c2) (t2 - t1) / log(c1 / c2)`;
* otherwise (rising, constant, or falling to zero): the linear trapezoid
  `(c1 + c2) (t2 - t1) / 2`.

Vectors of different lengths throw a `DimensionMismatch`; fewer than two
samples give `0.0`.

```julia
auc_linlog([0.0, 1.0, 3.0], [0.0, 8.0, 2.0])   # 4.0 + 8.656... = 12.656...
```

Results are compared with `rtol = 1e-12`: each interval is a few
operations, and a sum of positive terms in any order has a relative error
of about `n u`. On exactly exponential data the log trapezoid is exact, a
check you can run yourself. Speed and allocations are graded against the
reference.
problems.starter:
function auc_linlog(t, c)
    s = 0.0
    for i in 2:length(t)
        s += (c[i-1] + c[i]) / 2 * (t[i] - t[i-1])
    end
    return s
end
problems.title: AUC by the linear-up/log-down rule

hints: Gauss-Newton repeats: compute the residuals `r` and the Jacobian `J = ∂r/∂θ`, solve the linear least-squares problem `J δ ≈ -r` (with `\`), and step to `θ + δ`.

With `k = CL / V`, `log C = log(D k_a) - log V - log(k_a - k) + log(exp(-k t) - exp(-k_a t))`. Its derivative in `k` is `1/(k_a - k) - t exp(-k t) / (exp(-k t) - exp(-k_a t))`; the residual has the opposite sign, and `log V` also appears directly.
problems.prompt:
After one oral dose `D` (mg), a one-compartment model with known
absorption rate `k_a` predicts the concentration (the Bateman function)

    C(t) = D k_a / (V (k_a - k)) · (exp(-k t) - exp(-k_a t)),     k = CL / V

Write `fit_clearance(t, c, dose, ka, CL0, V0)` that fits `CL` and `V` to
measured concentrations `c` at times `t` (both `Vector{Float64}`, all
`c > 0`) by **Gauss-Newton** on the log residuals
`r_i = log c_i - log C(t_i)`, with the parameters `θ = (log CL, log V)`,
starting from `(CL0, V0)`. Halve a step while it does not reduce
`sum(r.^2)`, and stop when the step's norm is below `1e-10` (or after 100
iterations). Return the fitted `CL` as a `Float64`.

```julia
t = [0.5, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24]
c = [100 * 1.5 / (20 * (1.5 - 0.25)) * (exp(-0.25s) - exp(-1.5s)) for s in t]   # CL = 5, V = 20, no noise
fit_clearance(t, c, 100.0, 1.5, 7.5, 14.0)                                     # 5.0 (to 1e-10)
```

The Jacobian can be written by hand (differentiate `log C` with respect to
`k`, then use `∂k/∂log CL = k` and `∂k/∂log V = -k`) or by finite
differences. Every case starts within about a factor 1.5 of the minimum and has
`k_a` at least 3 times `k`. Results are compared with `rtol = 1e-6`: any
method that converges to the minimum of this sum of squares to `1e-8`
agrees with the reference, while minimizing the residuals `c_i - C(t_i)`
without the logarithm gives another minimum, off by more than `1e-3` on
the noisy cases.
problems.title: Fit the clearance by Gauss-Newton

sections.body:
Pharmacokinetics (PK) describes how the concentration of a drug in the
body changes after doses. This case study puts several earlier tools
together on one model. It relies on five facts:

* **A `DiscreteCallback` with `tstops`** changes the state at known times:
  the solver is made to stop exactly there, and the callback's condition
  is checked at the end of each step (unit 24, section "Events and
  callbacks: a bouncing ball").
* **`abstol` and `reltol` bound each step's local error estimate**, and the
  global error ends up somewhat larger, so an answer is checked against an
  exact one with a margin (unit 31, sections "What an adaptive solver's
  error estimate is" and "Work-precision: what a tolerance buys").
* **A linear system `u' = K u` has time scales `1/|λ|`** for the
  eigenvalues `λ` of `K`, and widely spread ones make it stiff (unit 35,
  section "Stability is set by the Jacobian's eigenvalues").
* **A Monte Carlo mean has a 95% interval `± 1.96 s / sqrt(N)`**, and an
  ensemble draws its random inputs reproducibly (unit 37, sections "Monte
  Carlo error and confidence intervals" and "Ensembles: many solves,
  reproducibly").
* **Local optimizers find local answers**: one nonconvex model from two
  starts can give two results (unit 38, section "Ipopt is local: one
  model, two answers"). A least-squares step is solved by QR, as in unit 32,
  section "Least squares: QR, not the normal equations".

**What this unit is not.** Real pharmacometric analyses fit
**population** models (nonlinear mixed-effects, NLME) to data from many
patients at once, with dedicated tools: Pumas (from PumasAI, a commercial
product with an academic access programme, [pumas.ai](https://pumas.ai/))
or nlmixr2 (an R package for NLME models, licensed GPL,
[nlmixr2.org](https://nlmixr2.org/)). The model and its parameter values
here are invented for teaching, and the data are simulated from known
parameters, so every answer can be checked.
sections.title: What you need from earlier units

sections.body:
A **compartment** is a well-mixed volume in which the drug has one
concentration. The model has three amounts (in mg):

* `A_g`, the dose in the gut, absorbed at rate `k_a A_g` (first order);
* `A_c`, the drug in the **central** compartment (blood and well-perfused
  organs) of volume `V_1`, where it is measured as `C = A_c / V_1` and
  eliminated at rate `CL · C` (the **clearance** `CL`, in L/h, is the
  volume cleared per hour);
* `A_p`, the drug in a **peripheral** compartment (tissue) of volume
  `V_2`, exchanged with the central one by the inter-compartmental
  clearance `Q`.

Each flow is a clearance times the concentration it leaves from:

    A_g' = -k_a A_g
    A_c' =  k_a A_g - (CL + Q) / V_1 · A_c + Q / V_2 · A_p
    A_p' =  Q / V_1 · A_c - Q / V_2 · A_p

The right-hand side is linear: `u' = K u` with a constant 3×3 matrix `K`.
So the exact solution is `u(t) = exp(K t) u(0)`, which `exp` of a matrix
computes, and every concentration curve is a sum of three exponentials
`exp(λ t)` with the eigenvalues of `K`. They are `-k_a` (absorption) and two
others, the **distribution** phase (fast) and the **elimination** phase
(slow), and `log(2) / |λ|` is the half-life of each phase. The slowest one
sets how long the drug stays: after the peak, the terminal decline is a
straight line on a log scale with that slope.

With the values below the eigenvalues spread over a factor of about 60.
That is not stiff: an explicit method's stable step is set by the fastest
time scale (half an hour), and over a horizon of days that costs only a
few hundred steps, so `Tsit5` is the right choice. A model with rates
spread over many more orders of magnitude (a fast infusion, a metabolite
formed in seconds) would be stiff and call for `Rodas5P`, as in unit 35.

examples.caption: k_a = 2 /h, CL = 5 L/h, V_1 = 20 L, Q = 4 L/h, V_2 = 60 L and one 100 mg dose: the eigenvalues of `K`, the half-lives of the three phases, and `Tsit5` at tolerances `1e-10` against the exact `exp(K t) u(0)`.
examples.code:
using OrdinaryDiffEq, LinearAlgebra
ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = 2.0, 5.0, 20.0, 4.0, 60.0
function pk!(du, u, p, t)                         # u = [gut, central, peripheral] amounts in mg
    ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = p
    du[1] = -ka * u[1]
    du[2] = ka * u[1] - (CL + Q) / V1 * u[2] + Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[3] = Q / V1 * u[2] - Q / V2 * u[3]
end
K = [-ka 0 0; ka -(CL + Q)/V1 Q/V2; 0 Q/V1 -Q/V2]
λ = sort(eigvals(K))
println("eigenvalues (1/h): ", round.(λ; digits = 4))
println("half-lives (h):    ", round.(log(2) ./ abs.(λ); digits = 2))
u0 = [100.0, 0.0, 0.0]
sol = solve(ODEProblem(pk!, u0, (0.0, 72.0), [ka, CL, V1, Q, V2]), Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
exact(t) = exp(K * t) * u0
peak = maximum(exact(t)[2] for t in 0:0.1:72)
println("max |A_c - exact| / peak below 1e-8: ", maximum(abs(sol(t)[2] - exact(t)[2]) for t in 0:0.5:72) / peak < 1e-8)
println("C at 1, 6, 24, 72 h (mg/L): ", round.([sol(t)[2] / V1 for t in (1.0, 6.0, 24.0, 72.0)]; sigdigits = 4))
examples.notice: Notice the three phases: absorption with a half-life of 0.35 h, distribution 1.4 h and elimination 20 h; and that the ODE solution agrees with the matrix exponential to better than `1e-8` of the peak amount, the size the tolerances predict.

choices: The one of smallest magnitude, since its term decays last
The one of largest magnitude, since it dominates the solution
`-k_a`, since absorption feeds the central compartment
questions.explain: The concentration is a sum of terms `a_j exp(λ_j t)`. The terms with large `|λ|` die out first, so at late times only the slowest one is left, and `log C` is then a line with slope `λ`. Here that is the 20-hour elimination phase.
misconceptions: A large `|λ|` makes its term decay fastest; it dominates only the first moments, not the tail.

Absorption with `k_a = 2 /h` is the fastest phase here; after a few hours the gut is empty and `-k_a` no longer shows. (If absorption were the slowest process, the tail would follow it: that is called flip-flop kinetics. The fit below shows a related swap, of absorption with distribution.)
questions.prompt: Long after a dose, the log of the concentration falls along a straight line. Which eigenvalue of `K` gives its slope?

sections.title: Two compartments and an absorption depot: one linear system

sections.body:
A dose taken every 12 hours adds 100 mg to the gut at `t = 0, 12, 24, …`.
The state jumps there, so a solver must not step across a dose time: it
would integrate the smooth equations through the jump and never see it.
The pattern from unit 24 does it:

* put the first dose in `u0`;
* a `DiscreteCallback` whose condition is `t in dose_times` and whose
  `affect!` adds the dose to `integrator.u[1]`;
* `tstops = dose_times`, which makes the solver end a step exactly at each
  dose time, so the condition is checked there and comes out `true`.

Without `tstops` the steps end wherever the error control puts them, which
is almost never exactly at 12.0, and the doses are silently skipped. (The
DiffEqCallbacks package has a ready-made `PresetTimeCallback` that does
both at once; it is not in this course's environment, and the two-line
version shows what it does.)

Because the equations are linear, the exact answer for several doses is
the **superposition** of single doses, each shifted to its own time:
`u(t) = Σ_{t_d ≤ t} exp(K (t - t_d)) · [D, 0, 0]`. That is an independent
check of the callback.

examples.caption: Five doses of 100 mg every 12 h: the callback solution with `tstops`, the superposition of matrix exponentials, and the same callback without `tstops` (concentrations in mg/L, 6 digits).
examples.code:
using OrdinaryDiffEq, LinearAlgebra
ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = 2.0, 5.0, 20.0, 4.0, 60.0
function pk!(du, u, p, t)
    ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = p
    du[1] = -ka * u[1]
    du[2] = ka * u[1] - (CL + Q) / V1 * u[2] + Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[3] = Q / V1 * u[2] - Q / V2 * u[3]
end
dose_times = 12.0:12.0:48.0                        # the doses after the first
cb = DiscreteCallback((u, t, integrator) -> t in dose_times, integrator -> (integrator.u[1] += 100.0))
prob = ODEProblem(pk!, [100.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, 72.0), [ka, CL, V1, Q, V2])
sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(); callback = cb, tstops = dose_times, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
missed = solve(prob, Tsit5(); callback = cb, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-10)
K = [-ka 0 0; ka -(CL + Q)/V1 Q/V2; 0 Q/V1 -Q/V2]
superposed(t) = sum(exp(K * (t - td)) * [100.0, 0.0, 0.0] for td in [0.0; dose_times] if td <= t)
println("  t    callback   superposition   no tstops")
for t in (6.0, 30.0, 60.0, 72.0)
    println(rpad(t, 6), rpad(round(sol(t)[2] / V1; digits = 6), 11), rpad(round(superposed(t)[2] / V1; digits = 6), 16),
            round(missed(t)[2] / V1; digits = 6))
end
examples.notice: Notice that with `tstops` the solution matches the superposition in all digits shown at every time, and that without `tstops` only the first dose (the one in `u0`) is in the solution: the concentration after 30 h is a seventh of the right one, and no warning is printed.

choices: `DiscreteCallback` conditions are only checked at the initial time
`t in dose_times` compares floats with `==`, which is never true for `12.0`
Steps rarely end exactly at a dose time, where the condition is checked
questions.explain: A `DiscreteCallback` is tested at the end of every step. The adaptive step sizes put those ends at times like 11.73 and 12.41, so `t in dose_times` is false at all of them. `tstops` forces a step to end at each listed time, where the test is exact.
misconceptions: The condition is checked after every step, which is why `tstops` alone fixes it; the first dose is missing from the callback only because it was put in `u0` instead.
`12.0 == 12.0` is true: both are the same exactly representable float. With `tstops` the solver lands on exactly `12.0`, and the comparison succeeds.
questions.prompt: A dosing callback has the condition `t in dose_times`, but the solve is called without `tstops`. Why are the doses skipped?

sections.title: Repeated doses as callbacks

sections.body:
The **AUC**, `∫ C(t) dt`, measures total exposure to the drug, and it has a
simple exact value. Elimination removes drug at rate `CL · C(t)`, so over
all time it removes `CL · AUC_∞`; everything absorbed is eventually
eliminated, so `CL · AUC_∞ = D` for a dose `D` that is fully absorbed:

    AUC_∞ = D / CL

whatever `k_a`, `Q` and the volumes are. ("The amount eliminated by the
body = clearance × AUC", [AUC in pharmacokinetics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_under_the_curve_(pharmacokinetics)).)
That is why clearance is the parameter dosing is built around, and why it
is the parameter data determine best (next section).

Two ways to compute an AUC:

* **From the model**, by adding a fourth equation `AUC' = A_c / V_1` and
  reading its value at the end: the integral then has the solver's
  accuracy.
* **From measured samples**, as in a clinical study, by a trapezoid rule
  between sample times. The **linear-up/log-down** rule is the default of
  the PKNCA package for noncompartmental analysis: linear interpolation while
  the concentration rises, and logarithmic when it falls to a nonzero
  value ([PKNCA: AUC integration methods](https://stat.ethz.ch/CRAN/web/packages/PKNCA/vignettes/v23-auc-integration-methods.html)).
  If `C` decays exponentially from `c_1` to `c_2` over `Δt`, its integral
  is exactly `(c_1 - c_2) Δt / log(c_1 / c_2)`, while the straight line
  overestimates a convex decay. You will write this rule in a problem.

examples.caption: One 100 mg dose: the AUC from an extra ODE state, at 72 h and at 400 h against `D / CL = 20`; then the AUC over 0 to 72 h from 15 samples with the linear and the linear-up/log-down trapezoid rules (mg·h/L).
examples.code:
using OrdinaryDiffEq
function pk_auc!(du, u, p, t)                      # u = [gut, central, peripheral, AUC]
    ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = p
    du[1] = -ka * u[1]
    du[2] = ka * u[1] - (CL + Q) / V1 * u[2] + Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[3] = Q / V1 * u[2] - Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[4] = u[2] / V1                              # dAUC/dt = C
end
p = [2.0, 5.0, 20.0, 4.0, 60.0]
sol = solve(ODEProblem(pk_auc!, [100.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, 400.0), p), Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-12, reltol = 1e-10)
println("AUC 0-72 h from the ODE:  ", round(sol(72.0)[4]; digits = 4))
println("AUC 0-400 h from the ODE: ", round(sol(400.0)[4]; digits = 6), "   D / CL = ", 100 / 5)
ts = [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 72]
cs = [sol(t)[2] / 20.0 for t in ts]
linear = sum((cs[i] + cs[i+1]) / 2 * (ts[i+1] - ts[i]) for i in 1:length(ts)-1)
linlog = sum(cs[i+1] < cs[i] && cs[i+1] > 0 ? (cs[i] - cs[i+1]) * (ts[i+1] - ts[i]) / log(cs[i] / cs[i+1]) :
             (cs[i] + cs[i+1]) / 2 * (ts[i+1] - ts[i]) for i in 1:length(ts)-1)
println("linear trapezoid:         ", round(linear; digits = 4))
println("linear-up/log-down:       ", round(linlog; digits = 4))
examples.notice: Notice that the ODE's AUC at 400 h is `D / CL` to about `1e-6` (the part after 400 h is `exp(-0.0346 · 400)` of the total), and that on the samples the log-down rule is closer than the linear rule, which overestimates every falling stretch.
examples.output:
AUC 0-72 h from the ODE:  19.1241
AUC 0-400 h from the ODE: 19.99999   D / CL = 20.0
linear trapezoid:         19.3723
linear-up/log-down:       19.1126

choices: It halves, since the same amount is spread over twice the volume
It stays the same, since `AUC_∞ = D / CL` does not involve the volume
It doubles, since the drug stays longer in the body when the volume is larger
questions.explain: The peak concentration is lower and the decline slower (elimination rate `CL / V_1` per hour is halved), and the two effects cancel exactly in the integral: everything absorbed is eliminated at rate `CL · C`, so `CL · AUC_∞ = D`.
misconceptions: The peak is lower, but the concentration also falls more slowly, since the same clearance removes a smaller fraction of a larger amount each hour; the area does not change.
The drug does stay longer, but at a lower concentration; the balance `CL · AUC_∞ = D` fixes the area.
questions.prompt: A second patient has the same clearance but twice the central volume `V_1`. After the same single dose, what happens to `AUC_∞`?

questions.code:
c1, c2, dt = 8.0, 2.0, 2.0
round((c1 - c2) * dt / log(c1 / c2); digits = 3)
questions.explain: `(8 - 2) · 2 / log(4) = 12 / 1.386 = 8.656`. That is the exact integral of the exponential through the two points; the straight line gives `(8 + 2) / 2 · 2 = 10`, an overestimate, because a decaying exponential is convex.
misconceptions: That is the linear trapezoid, `(c_1 + c_2) / 2 · Δt`; the log-down rule integrates an exponential through the two points, which lies below the straight line.
That is `(c_1 - c_2) Δt / 2`, without the logarithm; the rule divides by `log(c_1 / c_2)`, here `log 4 ≈ 1.386`.
That divides by `2 log 4`; the rule is `(c_1 - c_2) Δt / log(c_1 / c_2)`, with no extra factor.
questions.prompt: The concentration falls from 8 to 2 mg/L between two samples 2 h apart. What does the log-down trapezoid give for that stretch (rounded to 3 digits)?

sections.title: Exposure: the area under the curve

sections.body:
Data: 15 concentrations after one 100 mg dose, simulated from the true
parameters with multiplicative noise, `c_obs = C(t) · exp(0.1 z)` with
`z` standard normal (a 10% error, as an assay might have). The fit asks
for the parameters `θ` that minimize the sum of squares of the
**log residuals** `r_i(θ) = log c_obs_i - log C(t_i; θ)`, which treats a
10% error at 0.05 mg/L like one at 3 mg/L. Each parameter is fitted as its
logarithm, which keeps it positive.

**The method: Gauss-Newton.** Linearize the residuals around the current
`θ`, `r(θ + δ) ≈ r(θ) + J δ` with the Jacobian `J = ∂r/∂θ`, and pick the
`δ` that minimizes the linear model's sum of squares: a linear
least-squares problem, solved by QR (`J \ -r`). If the step does not
reduce the sum of squares, halve it. Here `J` comes from central finite
differences of the ODE solution (step `h = 1e-6` in `log θ`). Its error is
about `1e-6` relative, and it comes from the solver, not from truncation:
the truncation error of a central difference is of order `h² = 1e-12`,
while each residual carries the solver's own error, about `1e-12`, which
the difference divides by `2h`. Gauss-Newton stops where `J̃ᵀ r = 0` for
this approximate `J̃`, so the point it returns is moved slightly from the
true minimum, by much less than the 4 digits printed; the sum of squares,
which is flat at a minimum, moves less still.

**Why not a solver from unit 38?** Optim is not in this environment, and
JuMP with Ipopt would need the ODE written as constraints on a time grid
(collocation), with the dose jumps placed in that grid: a sound method,
but a large model for five parameters. A least-squares problem has
structure that Gauss-Newton uses directly, and every step is a linear
solve from unit 32.

**What the data determine.** A fit is local, and here the model is not
fully identifiable from one oral dose: the absorption rate and a
disposition rate can swap roles and produce the same concentration curve.
The classical case is **flip-flop kinetics**, where absorption is slower
than elimination and the terminal slope belongs to absorption. The example
finds another swap: from two guesses it reaches two parameter sets with the
**same** sum of squares (to better than `1e-9` relative), in which the
absorption rate of one is the distribution rate of the other (about 2.27
and 0.454 per hour); the terminal rate is the same in both. Both have the
same clearance: `CL = D / AUC`, and the AUC is pinned down by the data
whichever phase is which. That is the parameter to trust, and it comes with
a standard error from the curvature, `sqrt(σ² (JᵀJ)⁻¹)`.

examples.caption: Gauss-Newton with step halving on log residuals, from two starting guesses, fitted to concentrations simulated with `StableRNG(2026)` (true k_a = 2, CL = 5, V_1 = 20, Q = 4, V_2 = 60). Values rounded to 4 digits; the standard error of CL relative.
examples.code:
using OrdinaryDiffEq, LinearAlgebra, StableRNGs
function pk!(du, u, p, t)
    ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = p
    du[1] = -ka * u[1]
    du[2] = ka * u[1] - (CL + Q) / V1 * u[2] + Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[3] = Q / V1 * u[2] - Q / V2 * u[3]
end
tobs = [0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 36, 48, 72]
prob = ODEProblem(pk!, [100.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, 72.0), ones(5))
conc(θ) = (q = exp.(θ); solve(remake(prob; p = q), Tsit5(); abstol = 1e-12, reltol = 1e-10, saveat = tobs)[2, :] ./ q[3])
ptrue = [2.0, 5.0, 20.0, 4.0, 60.0]
cobs = conc(log.(ptrue)) .* exp.(0.1 .* randn(StableRNG(2026), length(tobs)))
resid(θ) = log.(cobs) .- log.(conc(θ))
function jacobian(θ; h = 1e-6)                      # central differences in log θ
    J = zeros(length(tobs), length(θ))
    for k in eachindex(θ)
        e = zeros(length(θ)); e[k] = h
        J[:, k] = (resid(θ .+ e) .- resid(θ .- e)) ./ (2h)
    end
    return J
end
function gauss_newton(θ)
    for _ in 1:100
        r, J = resid(θ), jacobian(θ)
        δ = -(J \ r)                                # least-squares step by QR
        λ = 1.0
        while sum(abs2, resid(θ .+ λ .* δ)) > sum(abs2, r) && λ > 1e-6
            λ /= 2
        end
        θ = θ .+ λ .* δ
        norm(λ .* δ) < 1e-8 && break
    end
    return θ
end
println("start                          fit (ka, CL, V1, Q, V2)              sum of squares   SE(CL)/CL")
sse = Float64[]
for start in ([3.0, 8.0, 30.0, 6.0, 40.0], [0.5, 4.0, 10.0, 4.0, 60.0])
    θ = gauss_newton(log.(start))
    r, J = resid(θ), jacobian(θ)
    push!(sse, sum(abs2, r))
    σ² = sum(abs2, r) / (length(r) - length(θ))
    se = sqrt.(σ² .* diag(inv(J' * J)))             # standard errors of log θ = relative errors of θ
    println(rpad(string(start), 31), rpad(string(round.(exp.(θ); sigdigits = 4)), 37),
            rpad(round(sum(abs2, r); sigdigits = 8), 17), round(se[2]; sigdigits = 2))
end
println("sums of squares equal to 1e-9 relative: ", isapprox(sse[1], sse[2]; rtol = 1e-9))
examples.notice: Notice that the two fits have the same sum of squares but different `k_a`, `V_1`, `Q` and `V_2`: the second start found the solution in which absorption and distribution trade rates (`k_a ≈ 0.45`, the first fit's distribution rate). The clearance is the same in both, within about 4% of the true 5 L/h, and its standard error is about 4%: the data determine it, and not which phase is absorption.

choices: The fit with the larger `k_a`, since absorption is usually fast
Neither of them, since a fit that finds two minima must have a bug in its Jacobian
The average of the two `k_a` values, as a compromise
The clearance, which both agree on; `k_a` is not determined by these data
questions.explain: Equal sums of squares mean the data cannot tell the two parameter sets apart: an oral dose's curve is a sum of exponentials, and which rate is absorption is not visible in it (here absorption and distribution can trade rates). The clearance is fixed by the AUC, so it is identified. Separating `k_a` needs other data, such as an intravenous dose that bypasses absorption.
misconceptions: Prior knowledge can break the tie, but then it is an assumption to state, not something the fit found; the data support both values equally.
A wrong Jacobian would slow or stall the iterations, not produce two parameter sets with identical sums of squares; the model itself has two equally good fits.
The average of two equally good answers is not itself a minimum; it can fit far worse than either.
questions.prompt: Two fits from different starts end with the same sum of squares to `1e-9` relative, `k_a = 2.3` in one and `k_a = 0.45` in the other, and the same `CL`. What should you report?

sections.title: Fitting the model to concentrations

sections.body:
Patients differ. A common model makes each patient's clearance and volume
log-normal around typical values: `CL_i = CL · exp(η_i)` with
`η_i ~ N(0, ω²)`, so the spread is multiplicative (here `ω_CL = 0.3`,
about 30%, and `ω_V1 = 0.2`). Simulating 500 patients is an
`EnsembleProblem`, with every patient's parameters drawn up front from a
`StableRNG` so that patient `i` is the same however the ensemble runs.

Two different intervals come out of such a simulation, and they answer
different questions:

* A **prediction interval** for one patient, from the quantiles of the
  simulated values: 90% of patients have a concentration at 24 h between
  the 5% and 95% quantiles. It does not shrink with more simulations; it is
  the spread of the population.
* A **confidence interval** for a population mean, `m ± 1.96 s / sqrt(N)`
  (unit 37): how well 500 simulations estimate the mean. It shrinks like
  `1 / sqrt(N)`.

The mean exposure has an exact value to check the Monte Carlo against:
`AUC_∞ = D / CL_i`, so `E[AUC] = (D / CL) E[exp(-η)] = (D / CL) exp(ω² / 2)`,
from the mean of a log-normal variable. It is larger than `D / CL`: the
typical patient's AUC is not the average patient's. The ensemble integrates
to 400 h, not to infinity, so patients with a low clearance lose a little
of their tail: about `5e-4` of their AUC (`exp(λ · 400)` for the slowest eigenvalue `λ`) for the lowest clearance drawn
here, and about `1e-5` of the mean, far inside the Monte Carlo interval.

examples.caption: 500 simulated patients (`StableRNG(11)`, `ω_CL = 0.3`, `ω_V1 = 0.2`, one 100 mg dose): the mean AUC with its 95% Monte Carlo interval against the exact `E[AUC]`, and a 90% prediction interval for the concentration at 24 h (rounded to 3 digits).
examples.code:
using OrdinaryDiffEq, StableRNGs, Statistics
function pk_auc!(du, u, p, t)
    ka, CL, V1, Q, V2 = p
    du[1] = -ka * u[1]
    du[2] = ka * u[1] - (CL + Q) / V1 * u[2] + Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[3] = Q / V1 * u[2] - Q / V2 * u[3]
    du[4] = u[2] / V1
end
N = 500
rng = StableRNG(11)
CLs = 5.0 .* exp.(0.3 .* randn(rng, N))
V1s = 20.0 .* exp.(0.2 .* randn(rng, N))
prob = ODEProblem(pk_auc!, [100.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0], (0.0, 400.0), [2.0, 5.0, 20.0, 4.0, 60.0])
ens = EnsembleProblem(prob;
    prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> remake(prob; p = [2.0, CLs[ctx.sim_id], V1s[ctx.sim_id], 4.0, 60.0]),
    output_func = (sol, ctx) -> ((sol.u[end][4], sol(24.0)[2] / V1s[ctx.sim_id]), false))
sim = solve(ens, Tsit5(); trajectories = N, abstol = 1e-10, reltol = 1e-8)
aucs, c24 = first.(sim.u), last.(sim.u)
m, half = mean(aucs), 1.96 * std(aucs) / sqrt(N)
println("mean AUC ", round(m; digits = 2), " ± ", round(half; digits = 2), "; exact E[AUC] = ", round(20 * exp(0.3^2 / 2); digits = 2),
        "; inside: ", abs(m - 20 * exp(0.3^2 / 2)) < half)
println("90% prediction interval for C(24 h): ", round.(quantile(c24, [0.05, 0.95]); sigdigits = 3), " mg/L, median ",
        round(median(c24); sigdigits = 3))
examples.notice: Notice that the confidence interval for the mean AUC contains the exact value `20 exp(0.045) = 20.9`, which is above `D / CL = 20`, and that the prediction interval for `C(24 h)` spans a factor of about four: the variability between patients, which more simulations would describe better but not narrow.
examples.output:
mean AUC 20.81 ± 0.59; exact E[AUC] = 20.92; inside: true
90% prediction interval for C(24 h): [0.0735, 0.314] mg/L, median 0.158

choices: Both shrink by a factor of 10, since both are estimated from the simulations
Only the prediction interval shrinks, by about 10
Only the confidence interval shrinks, by about 10
questions.explain: The confidence half-width is `1.96 s / sqrt(N)`, so 100 times the simulations divide it by 10. The prediction interval is made of quantiles of the population's distribution; more simulations estimate those quantiles better but do not move them.
misconceptions: The prediction interval describes how much patients differ, which is a property of the population model (`ω`), not of the number of simulations.
The two are swapped: the `1/sqrt(N)` law applies to the estimate of the mean, while the spread between patients is fixed by `ω`.
questions.prompt: The ensemble is rerun with 50,000 patients instead of 500. What happens to the two intervals?

choices: `AUC = D / CL` is convex in `CL`, so low clearances weigh more
Monte Carlo error, which would vanish if the ensemble had many more patients
The ensemble's tolerances bias every computed AUC upwards by a few percent
questions.explain: `1/CL` is a convex function, so its mean over patients exceeds its value at the median patient (Jensen's inequality): a patient with half the clearance has twice the AUC, while one with twice the clearance has half, and the doubling outweighs the halving. For log-normal `CL` it is exactly `exp(ω²/2)`, here 4.6%.
misconceptions: The exact mean `(D / CL) exp(ω² / 2)` is above `D / CL` with no sampling at all; the Monte Carlo estimate converges to it, not to `D / CL`.
With tolerances `1e-8` each AUC is accurate to about `1e-6`; the 4.6% difference is a property of the population, not of the solver.
questions.prompt: Clearance varies log-normally around 5 L/h, so the median patient has `CL = 5`. Why is the mean AUC over patients larger than `D / 5`?

sections.title: Patient variability: an ensemble and a Monte Carlo interval

units.summary: A two-compartment model of a drug taken by mouth, from equations to answers: the linear system and its three phases, repeated doses as callbacks checked against a matrix-exponential superposition, exposure (AUC) from the solution and from sampled data, a Gauss-Newton fit to simulated noisy concentrations that finds two equally good answers (and the same clearance in both), and an ensemble over patients with a Monte Carlo interval checked against an exact mean. A teaching model: real pharmacometrics uses dedicated population (NLME) tools.
units.title: Case study: a pharmacokinetic model

hints: The starter puts each conductance on the diagonal, but a resistor between two nodes also couples them: node `i`'s equation contains `v_j` too.
For a resistor between nodes `i` and `j` (both nonzero), the current `(v_i - v_j)/R` leaves `i` and enters `j`. Write out which entries of row `i` and row `j` that touches, and with which sign.
problems.prompt:
Write `node_voltages(n, resistors, injections)` for a DC network of
resistors with nodes `1:n` and ground `0`. `resistors` is a vector of
tuples `(i, j, R)`: a resistor of `R` ohms between nodes `i` and `j`
(either may be `0`). `injections` is a `Vector{Float64}` of length `n`:
the current (in A) that a source pushes **into** each node. Stamp the
conductance matrix `G` (nodal analysis) and return the node voltages
`G \ injections` as a `Vector{Float64}`.

```julia
node_voltages(1, [(1, 0, 2.0)], [1.0])                    # [2.0]: 1 A through 2 Ω
node_voltages(2, [(1, 2, 1.0), (2, 0, 2.0)], [1.0, 0.0])  # [3.0, 2.0]
```

Every case connects every node to ground through some path, so `G` is
nonsingular, and its condition number is below `1e4`; results are compared
with `rtol = 1e-10`, a margin of more than a thousand over the solve's error
bound `κ u ≈ 1e-12` (unit 30). Speed is graded against the reference.
problems.starter:
function node_voltages(n, resistors, injections)
    G = zeros(n, n)
    for (i, j, R) in resistors
        i > 0 && (G[i, i] += 1 / R)
        j > 0 && (G[j, j] += 1 / R)
    end
    return G \ injections
end
problems.title: Node voltages of a resistor network

hints: The starter fills the generators in the order they are listed. The merit order is an order by cost.
`sortperm(cost)` gives the indices from cheapest to dearest; write each unit's output at its own index so the result stays in the original order. Check the demand first.
problems.prompt:
Write `merit_order(cost, cap, demand)` for vectors `cost` and `cap`
(`Vector{Float64}`, one entry per generator, all costs different) and a
`demand` in MW. Return the cheapest schedule as a `Vector{Float64}` in the
generators' original order: run the generators from cheapest to dearest,
each up to its capacity, until the demand is met.

Throw an `ArgumentError` if `demand` is negative or larger than
`sum(cap)`.

```julia
merit_order([40.0, 12.0, 25.0], [250.0, 300.0, 200.0], 600.0)   # [100.0, 300.0, 200.0]
merit_order([40.0, 12.0, 25.0], [250.0, 300.0, 200.0], 0.0)     # [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]
```

Results are compared with `rtol = 1e-12`: the schedule is a few
subtractions of the inputs, exact or within a rounding of them. Speed is
graded against the reference.
problems.starter:
function merit_order(cost, cap, demand)
    p = zeros(length(cost))
    left = demand
    for g in eachindex(cost)
        p[g] = min(cap[g], left)
        left -= p[g]
    end
    return p
end
